query: For high-entropy alloys, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs hardness and strength and why? Define a controlled comparison that would reveal the governing behavior, predict the observations relative to a baseline, state the limits within which the hypothesis should hold, identify evidence that would support it, and specify an observation that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In single‐phase high-entropy alloys such as CoCrFeMnNi, controlled plastic deformation induces dynamic amorphization of coarse grains at the surface, producing an ultra‐nanocrystalline layer that leads to an inverse Hall–Petch effect (i.e. a reduction in hardness and friction) relative to a conventionally annealed coarse-grained baseline.
generation.material_initial_state: As-cast, coarse-grained single-phase CoCrFeMnNi high-entropy alloy.
generation.intervention: Apply controlled plastic deformation under inert (ultra-high vacuum) conditions to promote dynamic amorphization.
generation.conditions: Experiments must be conducted in an environment that minimizes oxidation (e.g., ultra-high vacuum) and uses consistent deformation parameters to allow dynamic amorphization to occur.
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of an ultra‐nanocrystalline, amorphized near-surface layer.
generation.mechanism: The severe plastic deformation activates a dynamic amorphization process wherein the initial coarse grains transform into a highly defective amorphous/nanocrystalline structure. This change reduces the strength typically provided by conventional dislocation pile-up at grain boundaries, thereby reversing the classical Hall–Petch effect; the resulting microstructure exhibits lower hardness and friction.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the baseline annealed (coarse-grained) alloy, the plastically deformed sample should exhibit a distinctly lower hardness and reduced friction coefficient as measured by nanoindentation and tribological testing, respectively, due to the formation of the ultra‐nanocrystalline near-surface layer.
generation.baseline: An annealed, coarse-grained CoCrFeMnNi alloy without induced dynamic amorphization.
generation.boundary: This behavior is expected in single-phase high-entropy alloys (specifically CoCrFeMnNi) under deformation in inert environments. The hypothesis may not hold in oxidizing conditions, in multiphase alloys, or if the imposed deformation is insufficient to trigger dynamic amorphization.
generation.uncertainty: The precise quantitative changes in hardness and friction as well as the detailed strain/deformation thresholds required to induce dynamic amorphization remain uncertain and may vary with processing conditions.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of CoCrFeMnNi high-entropy alloy samples: one set remains in the annealed coarse-grained state (control) and the other undergoes controlled plastic deformation in an ultra-high vacuum to induce potential dynamic amorphization. Characterize both sets using high-resolution STEM to determine grain structure, perform nanoindentation tests to assess hardness, and carry out tribological testing to measure friction coefficients.
measurements: STEM imaging for grain size distribution and detection of amorphous/nanocrystalline layers
Tribometer tests for friction coefficient assessment
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the plastically deformed samples do not show a statistically significant reduction in hardness and friction coefficient relative to the baseline, along with the absence of an ultra‐nanocrystalline amorphous surface layer in STEM observations, then the dynamic amorphization hypothesis as governing hardness and strength is falsified.

cited_evidence.text:
Evidence of Inverse Hall-Petch Behavior and Low Friction and Wear in High Entropy Alloys

Abstract: AbstractWe present evidence of inverse Hall-Petch behavior for a single-phase high entropy alloy (CoCrFeMnNi) in ultra-high vacuum and show that it is associated with low friction coefficients (~0.3). Grain size measurements by STEM validate a recently proposed dynamic amorphization model that accurately predicts grain size-dependent shear strength in the inverse Hall-Petch regime. Wear rates in the initially soft (coarse grained) material were shown to be remarkably low (~10–6 mm3/N-m), the lowest for any HEA tested in an inert environment where oxidation and the formation of mixed metal-oxide films is mitigated. The combined high wear resistance and low friction are linked to the formation of an ultra-nanocrystalline near-surface layer. The dynamic amorphization model was also used to predict an average high angle grain boundary energy (0.87 J/m2). This value was used to explain cavitation-induced nanoporosity found in the highly deformed surface layer, a phenomenon that has been linked to superplasticity.Subject terms: Structural materials, Structural properties
